overview: Adnyamathanha people are the people of the rocks of South Australia’s Flinders Ranges. Their communities maintain connections to country through family knowledge, skilled work and cultural teaching. Pastoral settlement restricted movement and access to land, but community histories describe adaptation and continuing identity, not disappearance.

periods.title: Communities gather at Nepabunna
periods.summary: The community’s account places arrival at the present Nepabunna site in the 1930s, after earlier camps near Damper Hill and Ram Paddock. Pastoral occupation and unreliable water supplies shaped these movements.

periods.title: Nantawarrina becomes a protected area
periods.summary: Nantawarrina was declared Australia’s first Indigenous Protected Area on August 26, 1998. Nepabunna community members combined their ties to country with planning for environmental and cultural management.

periods.title: Native title recognized
periods.summary: Federal Court determinations on March 30, 2009 recognized Adnyamathanha native title in specified areas. The park determination records non-exclusive rights; it does not transfer every form of ownership across the entire region.

periods.title: Warratyi research published
periods.summary: Research at Warratyi reported a long sequence of occupation, worked bone, pigments and stone technology. The findings expanded archaeological knowledge of Australia’s arid interior while distinguishing dated objects from inferred uses.

periods.title: A culture guide and dictionary
periods.summary: Terrence and Josephine Coulthard published a guide combining language with cultural practices and history. Its preparation brought together knowledge from many speakers and Elders and support from the Mobile Language Team.

periods.title: Generations of carving exhibited
periods.summary: Mulka Yata / The Knowledge of Place brought work from generations of Adnyamathanha carvers into a museum exhibition. The presentation linked historical craft and trade with continuing artistic work.

items.text: At Warratyi rock shelter, dating of sediments, hearth charcoal and eggshells supported occupation around 49,000 years ago. Worked red ochre was identified on a silcrete tool in the oldest excavated unit. This is evidence of pigment handling in a specific archaeological context, without identifying a surviving painted design.

A sharpened bone point from Warratyi’s SU3 layer was dated by its context to about 40,000 to 38,000 years ago. Its shape resembles tools interpreted elsewhere as awls or needles for working skins. Manufacture is evident, while its precise task remains an interpretation from comparison.

Resin residues and associated polish on stone artefacts support attaching flakes to handles or shafts. At Warratyi, these traces reveal composite tools whose wooden components need not survive. Microscopic analysis adds evidence of manufacture that a stone’s shape alone may not provide.

sections.title: Everyday work, food and learning on country

items.text: Nepabunna’s community history recalls fathers and uncles working skillfully on pastoral stations. It also describes how leases forced people to camp together and curtailed travel. Paid station work and continued family life developed under those constraints, rather than replacing all earlier relationships with country.

Iga Warta’s food programme credits cooking knowledge passed down by the family’s mother. Its meals combine bush foods with adaptations such as kangaroo lasagne or meatloaf. Campfire offerings include damper and quandong jam. These examples show inherited knowledge being used creatively in a community-run enterprise.

The same programme teaches seasonal plant foods, ochre and local social history. Its explanation of Yura Muda connects land, ancestral journeys, behavior and belonging. Teaching takes place through Elders’ knowledge and encounters with country, bringing environmental understanding together with social responsibilities.

sections.title: Carving and the lives of objects

items.text: Museums Victoria’s Wapma figure, X 94829, is catalogued as made around 1930 in the Copley area. The wooden snake has an upturned body, cut surface patterns and a darkened head. Its maker is unrecorded, and its later collection date must not be mistaken for its production date.

The South Australian Museum describes Ted Coulthard trading carefully made walking sticks, snakes, lizards, boomerangs and shields while working with pastoralists. Its 2024 exhibition places that work within a continuing family tradition, including Kristian Coulthard’s carving near Blinman. Selling objects and transmitting cultural knowledge formed connected parts of this practice.

The Adnyamathanha Culture Guide and Language Book is jointly credited to Terrence and Josephine Coulthard. The Mobile Language Team describes a two-way dictionary alongside grammar, kinship, music and social history. The volume draws on many speakers and Elders, making their contributions part of a substantial resource for future learners.

Museums Victoria also identifies Aunty Lily Neville’s contribution through Adnyamathanha translations and publications. Her work includes songs, wordlists, family stories, observations of bush life and annotated drawings. Such records preserve forms of knowledge that a vocabulary list alone could not fully convey.

The Nantawarrina case study describes community planning for a property managed by Nepabunna people with traditional ties to it. Training covered environmental management, fencing, tourism, feral-animal control and identifying threatened species. These are practical skills used to care for country and sustain organized work.

Recorded management activities included revegetation, weed and feral-animal control, interpretation of sites and tracks, and maintaining visitor facilities. Work also provided water supplies for camps and huts. The programme combined cultural responsibilities with the routine infrastructure required for people to use and care for a place.

The 2009 park determination recognizes specified rights to access, camp, gather resources, conduct ceremonies and teach the significance of places, subject to its terms. These non-exclusive rights coexist with other interests. A native-title determination is legal recognition of defined rights, rather than a declaration that colonial dispossession never occurred.

ATLA’s 2013 report records the purchase of Wilpena Pound Resort and sets out objectives for Adnyamathanha employment and cultural tours. Its mission emphasizes cultural information shared by Adnyamathanha people. The purchase is a documented institutional achievement; the report’s employment targets are plans, not proof that every target was fulfilled.

ending.text: Adnyamathanha people continue to live on and care for their country through community life, cultural work and public institutions. Pastoral dispossession changed access and mobility, but did not end the people. The map’s 1815 endpoint is a coverage limit, not a verified conquest or extinction date.
